PpfBJrh6zQg.title: Kickoff
PpfBJrh6zQg.summary: In this kickoff session for Protocol School 2025, an unnamed orientation leader uses the bristlemouth fish (the most abundant vertebrate on Earth, yet unknown to most people) as a metaphor for how protocols pervade daily life unnoticed, introducing 'protocol watching' and 'protocol built' as practices for cultivating awareness. Tim then argues protocols are 'engineered arguments' that produce Whitehead advances, using an Ethereum flash-loan transaction and the concept of 'hardness' (atoms, institutions, now cryptography/code) to show how Ethereum functions as a 'mesoprotocolized world.' Timber closes by advocating a meso-level focus for protocol intervention, introducing the 'carrier bag theory of management,' tension-based protocol design, and a capability maturity model for AI adoption, alongside housekeeping for the week's certificate program.

Vh4awAsNGj8.title: Protocolized Modeling and Verification of Cyber Physical Systems - Giovanni Merlino
Vh4awAsNGj8.summary: Giovanni Merlino, professor of computer science engineering at the University of Messina, presents the redesigned final module of his cyber-physical systems (CPS) course, framing formal verification techniques—linear temporal logic (LTL), finite state machine equivalence/refinement, and model checking—as a form of 'protocolization' that makes hidden assumptions, tradeoffs, and human-machine interactions explicit. He walks through concepts like safety vs. liveness properties, simulation vs. bisimulation, the CEGAR (counter-example guided abstraction refinement) technique, and Büchi automata, ultimately proposing a layered model (robot-level, swarm-level, smart-city-level) where engineering tensions like hyper-safety vs. liveness or pedestrian priority vs. system efficiency require explicit governance levers.
key_concepts: finite state machine equivalence and refinement (bisimulation, simulation)
model checking and counter-example guided abstraction refinement (CEGAR)

n_geUireI5o.title: Beyond Consensus - Protocols as Digital Institutions - Martin Harrigan
n_geUireI5o.summary: Martin Harrigan, a lecturer and teaching fellow at SETU in Ireland, presents a method for using LLMs to study protocols: first building an LLM context file by transcribing and clustering ideas from the entire Summer of Protocols YouTube channel, then using that context plus a 10-property framework from 'The Unreasonable Sufficiency of Protocols' to roleplay protocols (like his 'Kevin the dinner host' example) and test properties such as defensibility, mortality, and legitimacy. He walks through building prompts, meta-prompting, and steering LLM conversations to demonstrate these properties, while noting weaknesses like circular reasoning and the difficulty of generalizing from a single instantiation.
key_concepts: ten properties of good protocols (constrained, generative, defensible, mortal, etc.)

VW3jTSFZ5z0.title: Designing Digital Worlds Communities, Protocols, AI, and Power - Andrés Monroy Hernández
VW3jTSFZ5z0.summary: Andrés Monroy-Hernández and Soyeon (So-young) outline a Princeton course on 'designing digital worlds,' tracing a lineage from Elinor Ostrom's commons governance and Yochai Benkler's commons-based peer production to today's decentralized social media protocols (ActivityPub, AT Protocol, Nostr, Farcaster), arguing each architecture encodes distinct political trade-offs around identity, curation, and infrastructure power. So presents her research on 'governance frictions' between federated communities and proposes design concepts like 'governance nutrition facts,' 'trust bubbles,' and an 'issue bulletin' to help fediverse moderators coordinate across incompatible norms.</br>
key_concepts: commons-based peer production vs. common-pool resource governance
power over identity/curation/infrastructure in decentralized social media
Lessig's pathetic dot theory and Creative Commons

ve0oe09LhI0.title: Musicalization not Music - Ben Zucker
ve0oe09LhI0.summary: Ben Zucker presents 'Musicalization not Music,' arguing that Western musical notation functions as a protocol in the formal sense—a symbolization (per Lawrence Halprin) that organizes behavior for 'reliable repeatability' while leaving emergent, implicit layers of performance practice to flourish around it. Drawing on Nelson Goodman's notational schemes, Brian Eno, and the Protocol Reader (including Tajuddin's 'phenomenal protocols'), Zucker proposes a framework of parameters—differentiation, discreteness, sufficiency, efficiency vs. thoroughness—for analyzing any protocol's explicit notation against its lore-based implicit practices, then extends this to 'musicalization': applying musical time, embodiment, and aesthetic attention to everyday and ecological protocols like doing laundry or airport security.

mK9R4hDyBgo.title: Designing Trust Protocols, Society, and Web 3.0 - Helena Rong
mK9R4hDyBgo.summary: Helena Rong, assistant professor at NYU Shanghai, previews her spring 2026 course on trust protocols for the agentic web, introducing 'trust experience design' as a framework with three layers—evidence (cryptographic attestations), primitives (verifiable credentials, zero-knowledge proofs), and rituals/experience (signals that make trust felt). She traces trust's evolution from value-based/social forms (handshakes, institutions) to proof-based/technical forms (blockchains, smart contracts), and discusses decentralized AI agents (DeAgents) like Truth Terminal and Sporef.fun as cases of emerging AI self-sovereignty that outpace existing trust protocols like A2A and ERC-8004. The session concludes with a group exercise where participants design trust protocols for near-future scenarios like autonomous mobility, smart grids, and robotic surgery.
key_concepts: hardness (cost to corrupt a trusted system)
agentic web trust protocols (A2A, ERC-8004, know-your-agent)

quqfI_fiTJw.title: Protocol Design as Governance - Eric Alston
quqfI_fiTJw.summary: Eric Alston presents a curriculum module for his blockchain and finance students, arguing that protocol design functions as governance across four domains: standards, networks, complexity/uncertainty, and constitutive choice. He draws on readings from David Lang, Venkatesh Rao, and his own institutional economics work to argue that protocols are a 'scalar mechanism' for human coordination, distinguishing institutions (exogenously enforced, foreseeable rules) from norms (emergent, ubiquitous constraints), and uses modularity theory to explain how complex systems 'imprison' complexity within subsystems via constitutional-like interfaces.

lkK5rlc5zMM.title: Strategy as an Organizational Coordination Protocol for the Public Sector - Vaughn Tan
lkK5rlc5zMM.summary: Vaughn Tan presents a prototype session from a new executive-education course on public sector strategy, arguing that strategy should be redefined as 'making reasoned subjective arguments about acceptable trade-off configurations' rather than planning or objective-setting, framing it explicitly as a coordination protocol for decentralized hierarchies. He critiques how public sector strategy has inherited mid-20th-century American private-sector frameworks (business policy model, SWOT, NPM) ill-suited to public contexts, illustrates coordination failures via Grenfell Tower and desert-city flooding, and introduces the Knightian risk/uncertainty distinction (using WHO's COVID travel-restriction guidance) to argue public servants mismanage uncertainty by treating it as calculable risk. He also proposes 'parametric cases'—short, highly localized, content-specific teaching cases—as a pedagogical fix for traditional long, decontextualized business-school case studies.
key_concepts: strategy as a coordination protocol for decentralized hierarchies
private-sector strategy frameworks misapplied to public sector (NPM, SWOT, resource-based view)

ZVYlO6xsEa4.title: Protocols of Storytelling - Qiufan Stanley Chen
ZVYlO6xsEa4.summary: Stanley Qiufan Chen, author of Waste Tide and co-author with Kai-Fu Lee of AI 2041, teaches a workshop on 'protocols of storytelling,' arguing that meaning in fiction emerges from a shared protocol-space between author and reader—genre conventions, causal layer analysis (Sohail Inayatullah's four layers: litany, systemic causes, worldview, myth/metaphor), and a 'constraint-driven focus' that keeps every narrative choice traceable back to a story's core idea. He guides participants through an iterative 'seed-root-flower-fruit' exercise, using works like The Matrix, Evangelion, and Arrival to show how deep protocols (myth, worldview) are harder to change than surface elements (plot, imagery), and how human-first, AI-assisted co-writing can deepen rather than flatten speculative fiction.

RQZGImdwpYQ.title: Towards a New Social Science of Protocols - Yige Wang
RQZGImdwpYQ.summary: Yige Wang (going by 'IU'), a sociologist, presents the design of a new undergraduate course 'Toward a Social Science of Protocol,' structured around core theoretical lenses (functionalism, conflict theory, symbolic interactionism), micro-level linguistic/pragmatic protocols like Grice's cooperative principle, and macro-level historical analysis using Norbert Elias's 'The Civilizing Process' and Chinese vs. Western civilizational protocol divergence (protocol pluralism vs. protocol monoculture). She runs live interactive experiments with the audience (cross-disciplinary paraphrasing exercise, Zoom chat protocol-spotting) to demonstrate implicit versus explicit protocols in real time.
key_concepts: civilizing process and etiquette as embodied protocol

qIhMQBaJ3ug.title: Protocol Art I - Primavera De Filippi & Felix Beer
qIhMQBaJ3ug.summary: Primavera De Filippi introduces 'protocol art' as a conceptual framework distinguishing autographic works (made directly by the artist) from allographic, protocol-based works where an artist designs rules that others instantiate with their own creative discretion, citing Sol LeWitt, Lazlo Moholy-Nagy, and Niele Toroni as historical precedents. She traces how blockchain, generative AI, and digital platforms (e.g., her own Plantoids, Olus's voice-cloning project, and Million Dollar Homepage) expand protocol art's design space, and proposes taxonomic axes—atomic vs. systemic, strict vs. fluid, technical vs. social—for classifying works, while fielding audience questions on discretionary space, copyright implications, and genericide of recognizable protocols.

EuuTlDAQEr0.title: Protocol Art II - Primavera De Filippi & Felix Beer
EuuTlDAQEr0.summary: Primavera De Filippi leads a seminar on protocol art, working through audience case studies (role-playing games, choreography, Yanis Xenakis scores, PostSecret, Pak's Merge/Censored) to test the boundaries between protocol-as-tool, protocol-as-medium, and mere mimetic/meme art. She then presents two archetypal case studies, Oli Plus and Plantoid, analyzing distributed authorship, asynchronous collaboration, DAO-based governance, the limits of copyright versus personality rights, automated royalty systems, community roles, and the temporal/evolutionary nature of protocol-based artworks.
key_concepts: protocol art vs. protocol as tool/medium
distributed authorship between protocol artist and instantiating artist
asynchronous, permissionless collaboration via smart contracts and DAOs
autographic vs. allographic works and copyright limits in protocol art
case studies: Oli Plus (AI voice protocol) and Plantoid (blockchain-based generative sculpture)

sjIAcXuspBE.title: Applied Protocol Thinking - Timber Stinson-Schroff
sjIAcXuspBE.summary: Timber Stinson-Schroff closes Protocol School 2025 with a capstone talk on 'Applied Protocol Thinking,' arguing that protocol literacy is best built through 'protocol watching'—a low-intensity, habitual practice analogous to an endurance athlete's easy-pace training—before attempting high-stakes protocol design. He introduces frameworks like hazard-oriented protocoling (analogous to object-oriented programming), the Chesterton's Fence vs. Gordian Knot heuristic, and Erik Hollnagel's ETTO (efficiency-thoroughness trade-off) principle reframed as an ongoing tension to manage rather than solve, illustrating concepts with examples from dog-walking, library shelving carts, tree-trimming crews, and GitLab's engineering trade-offs.
key_concepts: protocol watching as a practice (umarellos/field guide)
Chesterton's Fence vs. Gordian Knot heuristic
ETTO principle (efficiency-thoroughness trade-off) as managed tension
hazard-oriented protocoling (HOP, modeled on object-oriented programming)

6KpWypVFL2o.title: Bridge Atlas - Episode 1: Intro | Tim Beiko & Timber Stinson-Schroff
6KpWypVFL2o.summary: In this launch episode of the Bridge Atlas series, host Christine Kim talks with Tim Beiko (Ethereum Foundation) and Timber Stinson-Schroff (Summer of Protocols project manager) about the origins of Summer of Protocols, which Beiko initiated with Venkatesh Rao to find a framework for understanding Ethereum beyond analogy, landing on 'protocols' and 'engineered arguments' as the unifying concept. They discuss key concepts developed over three years—like Nadia Asparouhova's Kafka index for evaluating protocols by their worst failure modes, and Whitehead advances describing how successful protocols disappear into the background—and explain that Bridge Atlas aims to connect Ethereum's protocol engineers with Summer of Protocols alumni from unrelated fields (coal mining safety, wildfire management) ahead of a culminating event at Devconnect.

GUxwGds2uJU.title: Bridge Atlas - Episode 2: Paradigms | Nils Gilman and Josh Stark
GUxwGds2uJU.summary: Nils Gilman (Berggruen Institute) and Josh Stark (Ethereum Foundation) discuss two concepts they each coined: 'planetary thinking' (governance of non-human-directed flows like carbon, whales, and space debris) and 'hardness' (a system's capacity to make future outcomes reliably true, distinct from subjective trust or reliance). They explore how hardness explains Ethereum's appeal amid declining institutional trust, distinguish hardness from trust using examples like universities versus Harvard's reputation, and discuss Ethereum's potential role in planetary-scale coordination through projects like Rarimo's Freedom Tool and Bhutan's national ID system.

4xZSeujEmig.title: Bridge Atlas - Episode 3: Commons | Yancey Strickler & Trent Van Epps
4xZSeujEmig.summary: Host Christine Kim talks with Trent Van Epps (Ethereum Foundation, Protocol Guild) and Yancey Strickler (Metalabel, Artist Corporations) about Ethereum and creative work as 'commons.' Van Epps explains Protocol Guild's legibility strategy of bundling 200 core developers to attract funding via mechanisms like the 1% pledge, while Strickler describes using label structures, revenue splits, and a proposed legal form (the Artist Corporation) to let creative groups share governance and money without full financialization.
key_concepts: Metalabel revenue splits and group treasuries

zHGghwyrZzY.title: Bridge Atlas - Episode 4: Alignment | Emmett Shear & Alex Stokes
zHGghwyrZzY.summary: Emmett Shear (founder of Softmax) argues that alignment is not a fixed state but a relative, multi-scale protocol built on shared success, specialization, and only then enforcement, and warns that a single global, fork-resistant blockchain or AI system would be dangerous because it eliminates the ability to exit or locally reinterpret rules. Alex Stokes (Ethereum Foundation) counters that Ethereum's decentralization and permissionlessness push power to the edges, using rollups and the ability to fork as mechanisms to avoid Shear's feared 'ossified' lock-in, while the two debate whether Ethereum or any man-made protocol can sustain genuine, evolving alignment the way Shear argues organic systems do via Karl Friston's free energy principle.
key_concepts: alignment as protocol (shared success, specialization, enforcement)

BPsgkqgTWos.title: Bridge Atlas - Episode 5: Verifiability | Shreya Shankar & Justin Drake
BPsgkqgTWos.summary: Shreya Shankar (Berkeley PhD, creator of the DocETL declarative data-processing system) and Justin Drake (Ethereum Foundation, lean Ethereum project) compare verifiability across AI data pipelines and blockchain consensus. Drake explains SNARKs, trust-minimization, and recursive proof composition for Ethereum's deterministic and non-deterministic components, while Shankar details how DocETL handles LLM-powered query pipelines, human-AI misalignment, and eval design for unstructured data like court transcripts, with both drawing parallels between 'hints' in SNARK proving and decomposition techniques for AI reasoning verification.
key_concepts: optimistic vs ZK rollups and trust spectrum
AI eval design and human-AI misalignment
formal verification and economic penalties for malicious actors

QZwciILmsx8.title: Centaur Fiction with Qiufan Chen & Amita Shukla
QZwciILmsx8.summary: Qiufan Chen (referred to as 'Stanley' in the session) discusses with Amita Shukla his multi-model LLM pipeline for fiction writing—using Gemini for long-context novel-length editing, Claude for nuanced language, and GPT variants for ideation—while insisting that trained writerly 'taste' must filter and rewrite every AI output rather than accept it directly. He describes AI as an 'exoskeleton' that augments but doesn't replace authorial intention, illustrates this with his branching-narrative immersive theater production in Hong Kong, and argues writers must craft new hopeful metaphors (solarpunk) to reshape climate storytelling.
key_concepts: multi-model LLM writing pipeline (Gemini, Claude, GPT)
taste and intuition as human filter for AI output

iwqoeIMXuzU.title: Beyond Consensus: Protocols as Digital Institutions
iwqoeIMXuzU.summary: Martin Harrahan (a teaching fellow at Southeast Technological University in Ireland) presents a protocol school workshop demonstrating an LLM-powered pipeline that transcribes and clusters the Summer of Protocols YouTube corpus into 'foundational' and 'aggregated' ideas, which can then be loaded as context to get chatbots to answer in protocol-studies terms rather than narrow computer-science definitions. He then walks participants through using an LLM persona ('Kevin the dinner host') to roleplay a chosen protocol and test it against the ten properties from Josh Stark's 'Unreasonable Sufficiency of Protocols' framework (e.g. defensibility, mortality, hardness), showing how conversational steering can reveal whether a protocol resists capture or can gracefully die out.
key_concepts: ten properties of a good protocol (constrained, generative, learnable, legible, ludic, stewardable, defensible, evolvable, mortal, legitimate)
roleplaying protocols with LLMs as a sparring/analysis technique

-5Lq2uaOgBw.title: Nathan Schneider: Contributions to a Glossary of Protocol
-5Lq2uaOgBw.summary: Nathan Schneider, a media studies professor writing a book on protocols for MIT Press, argues that Alexander Galloway's influential 2004 'Protocol' framed protocols purely as top-down control and is historically inaccurate, proposing instead a broad definition of protocols as 'patterns of interaction' that includes vernacular, non-elite protocol-making (developed with Avery Edenfield) and protocol sovereignty/capture dynamics (developed with Johannes Bunke). He also discusses his Protocol Oral History Project interviewing quilters, choreographers, and diplomats, his concept of 'implicit feudalism' in online governance, and a closing debate with Venkatesh Rao over whether centering indigenous/diasporic knowledge in protocol theory is legitimate pluralism or ideological social constructionism.
key_concepts: protocols as patterns of interaction (vs. Galloway's control-based definition)

Sh61GUPaWUI.title: Cosmopolis, Metropolis, Nation-State: 3 Protocols for Articulating Civilizational Memory
Sh61GUPaWUI.summary: Venkatesh Rao presents a research talk introducing 'cosmopolis' as a third geographic logic—alongside territorial (nation-state) and nodal (metropolis) logics—defined as a geography shaped by a way of life induced by major technology, arguing that cosmopolitical/behavioral logic is where civilizational memory is most robustly carried since territories and cities 'can forget' but cosmopolises 'truly remember.' He builds a framework of soil/stack/virtual-soil embodiments and effective/declarative/procedural memory types, applying it to historical cases (print culture, Islamic world, chivalry) and emerging computational cosmopolises (blockchain, AI, IoT, VR) to argue that behavioral-logic-driven 'protocols of circulation' offer a livable alternative to monolithic centralized or oozifying nodal futures.
key_concepts: territorial vs nodal vs behavioral logic
habitus and noosphere as components of cosmopolitical memory
articulation of civilizational memory (effective, declarative, procedural)
monolithic vs oozifying vs circulatory protocols of memory

rYhAkVFRbjo.title: The State of Climate Protocols
rYhAkVFRbjo.summary: Cory Levenson (Corey Levenson), an engineer and climate tech consultant previously with Regen Network, surveys the state of carbon dioxide removal (CDR) protocols, distinguishing 'closed system' pathways like direct air capture and biochar (easy MRV, high cost) from 'open system' pathways like enhanced rock weathering and ocean alkalinity enhancement (cheaper but harder to quantify due to attribution challenges). He details emerging data protocols—including the Carbon Data Open Protocol, Cascade's ERW Data Query, and Carbon to Sea's Ocean Alkalinity Enhancement Data Protocol—and argues the field should adopt community-governed standards bodies (like OBO Foundry or schema.org's science working group) rather than letting registries like Isometric capture scientific protocol development.
key_concepts: open vs closed system carbon removal pathways
durable CDR and voluntary carbon markets

13P3U6Xm6Mk.title: Charity Majors: Observability
13P3U6Xm6Mk.summary: Charity Majors, co-founder of Honeycomb, discusses with interviewer Benat (Venkatesh Rao) how observability emerged from her and co-founder Christine's experience with Facebook's Scuba tool, defining it via control theory as understanding internal system state from outputs, and distinguishing it from traditional monitoring through high-cardinality, high-dimensionality data capture. They explore how this concept applies beyond software to protocol governance broadly, using examples like tsunami warning networks and the LEAF Coalition's use of satellite data plus chainsaw-detecting microphones to monitor Amazon deforestation compliance, with Majors emphasizing that the key is capturing enough high-cardinality data to ask novel questions later and tailoring the 'story' to the audience's capacity for action.

fKqNSE9NmGU.title: The Infinite Game of Poetry: Protocols for Living, Listening, and Transcending the Rules
fKqNSE9NmGU.summary: Poet and technologist Robert Peake presents a framework for poetry as a form of protocol and 'protocoling,' arguing that poetry is an infinite, unwinnable game defined by Marvin Bell's dictum: 'learn the rules, break the rules, make up new rules, and break the new rules.' Drawing on Gödel's incompleteness theorem, Bertolt Brecht, and examples like William McGonagall's disastrous verse versus ChatGPT-generated poetry, Peake distinguishes first-order protocols (grammar, form) from second-order 'protocoling' (the recursive, self-breaking evolution of rules), framing poetry as a compression algorithm that uses words to transcend words.
key_concepts: poetry as compression algorithm and infinite game
Marvin Bell's rule-breaking algorithm of craft
tension and quarrel as generative poetic mechanism

q6SRoqp1vJQ.title: AI as Normal Technology
q6SRoqp1vJQ.summary: Arvind Narayanan presents his paper/book 'AI as Normal Technology,' arguing against superintelligence narratives by applying innovation-diffusion theory (invention, innovation, diffusion stages) to AI, contending that societal adoption is bottlenecked by slow organizational, business-model, and institutional adaptation rather than by the pace of capability gains. In discussion with Venkatesh Rao, they connect this to protocol theory, framing workflows, business models, and context engineering practices as new 'protocols' that must be invented, while Rao draws analogies to naval warfare tactics, printing-press literacy, and the hardness/mud distinction from Josh Stark's work to explain why protocol adoption is inherently slow but durable.
key_concepts: AI as normal technology vs. superintelligence

tNYQcWksOro.title: Protocol Fiction Panel + Contest Announcement
tNYQcWksOro.summary: This town hall announces the 'Ghosts and Machines' protocol fiction contest and features Stanley Chen (author of Waste Tide) teaching a 'deep writing' method using Causal Layer Analysis to build stories across plot, systemic causes, worldview, and myth. Sam Chua presents the Southeast Asia workshop, including a protocol design fiction canvas and an essay on distributed AI inspired by Balinese subak irrigation systems, zodiac-based AI allocation, family heirloom devices, and AI-infused 'haunted' forests, followed by a panel with Chen, Chua, and Venkatesh Rao discussing scene-making, Astounding Magazine's history, and advice for contest entrants to seek surreal realism and 'surprising agency' in their stories.

yXK2nEw7lM8.title: Into the Spannungsfeld (SIG Kickoff)
yXK2nEw7lM8.summary: Robert Peake kicks off his special interest group on the 'Spanungsfeld' (field of tensions), building on tension-mapping workshops from Edge City Esmeralda and Edge City Lana, and drawing on landscape theory of aggregation to argue that organizations and protocols must be understood as fields of coupled trade-offs and social conflicts rather than isolated engineering decisions. Venkatesh Rao joins to extend the discussion with concepts like agonistics, emotional homeostasis in organizations, cursed problems in game design, Schelling's micromotives and macro behavior, and the idea of 'unmanaged tension fields,' proposing that protocols function as tools for decoupling complex systems and managing chronic, unsolvable tensions rather than solving them outright.
key_concepts: tension games / tensions as partially solved arguments
unmanaged tension fields and cascading failures

RVFoRVBvW7E.title: Towards a Formal Theory of Protocols
RVFoRVBvW7E.summary: Venkatesh Rao (referred to as Benitesh Raalo in the transcript) launches a technical-foundations track for the Protocol Institute, proposing to formalize protocol studies the way control theory formalized manufacturing or general equilibrium theory formalized economics. He walks through worked examples—handwashing as a 'micro protocol' modeled via finite automata and grammar rules, and his own 2004-2006 Air Force battlespace simulation work using region connection calculus and temporal interval calculus—to illustrate how protocols might be formalized across a 'basket of protocols' ranging from Ethereum to royal court etiquette. Timber Stinson-Schroff co-hosts, announcing a parallel 'tension field theory' special interest group and a six-month study group culminating in a fall 'Basket of Protocols' workshop.
key_concepts: region connection calculus / temporal interval calculus

07_1FegA1Gg.title: Protocols in Electronic Design
07_1FegA1Gg.summary: Engineer Vikram Shaker (Qualcomm RF front-end) surveys protocols across electronic design, from hard standards like NIST's cesium-clock definition of the second and the 50-ohm coaxial impedance convention, to communication standards (USB, chiplet interconnects like UCIe and CXL), validation failures (Intel's Pentium FDIV bug and the resulting birth of formal verification), and documentation disasters (NASA's Mars Climate Orbiter unit mismatch). He frames these through Protocol Institute concepts like 'tension' versus 'trade-off' and the efficiency-thoroughness (ETO) frontier, and closes by examining unwritten cultural, ethical, and geopolitical protocols governing chip industry work.

KcICTT2GJY0.title: Intro to Protocol Studies: Argument Engineering for Dummies
KcICTT2GJY0.summary: A Summer of Protocols instructor delivers an introductory lecture framing protocols as 'engineered arguments' that manage ongoing tensions between agents rather than solve problems outright, walking through core vocabulary like strata, loci, Whitehead advance, the Kafka index, protocolization debt, and hardened commons. He illustrates these concepts with case studies including Jiordi Rosales and Nathalia Scherer's work on prescribed-burn approval in Sonoma County, Celeste LeCompte and Danielle Butler's research on urban flood classification protocols, and examples like the LEAP peanut-allergy program and Texas grid privatization versus California's automated demand response.

yBc7IxHT38M.title: Emmett Shear: Alignment Protocols
yBc7IxHT38M.summary: Emmett Shear, founder of Softmax and former interim CEO of OpenAI, argues that alignment is not a static property but a capability built through a protocol stack: shared success (biological stress-sharing like reactive oxygen species), specialization (cellular differentiation, corporate job roles), and enforcement (immune systems, auditors) — in that order. He critiques mainstream AI safety for starting with enforcement and control rather than cultivating mutual care and interdependence from small-scale interactions upward, advocating multi-agent rather than singleton AI architectures.
key_concepts: shared success via stress-sharing (reactive oxygen species)

JjVj_WRXxwA.title: Public Intelligence
JjVj_WRXxwA.summary: Kevin Kelly, Wired co-founder, presents his essay 'Public Intelligence,' arguing AI should be built as a commons like the internet or Wikipedia rather than owned by corporations or nations—combining public access, accountability, data (the 'omnipedia'), funding, and participation. In the Q&A moderated by Venkatesh Rao at a Bangkok town hall, Kelly argues decentralized AI will require corporate risk-taking to prove viability before being 'returned' to public commons, and identifies failure modes including fragmentation into competing sovereign national AIs and technical infeasibility of planetary-scale federated intelligence.
key_concepts: sovereign AI vs. global public intelligence

2OyZt4gbUNA.title: The Intersubjective Consensus Problem
2OyZt4gbUNA.summary: Sriram, founder of EigenLayer and University of Washington faculty, explains to Venkatesh Rao how blockchains function as 'verifiable commitment' engines, tracing the evolution from Bitcoin's narrow commitments (coin ownership, fixed supply) to Ethereum's Turing-complete generalization, and then identifies a core gap: blockchains cannot natively verify off-chain facts like GPU inference results, asset prices, or election outcomes. He introduces EigenLayer's restaking model and 'intersubjective consensus' mechanism—using forking tokens and escalating staker adjudication—as a solution for settling social truths (e.g., oracle disputes, prediction market resolution) that fall between pure mathematical verifiability and purely subjective taste.

Ze9pqaIrebY.title: Fireside Chat with Nadia Asparouhova
Ze9pqaIrebY.summary: In this fireside chat, Nadia Asparouhova discusses the concept of anti-memes—ideas that resist spreading or being remembered—drawing on SCP fiction and her book Anti-Mimetic. She extends an epidemiological analogy to online communities, critiquing Venkatesh Rao's 'cozy web' concept by comparing group chats to poorly-ventilated COVID pods that compress and mutate ideas rather than truly insulating people from them, and connects her SOP23 essay's 'Whitehead protocol' (good, attention-freeing automation) versus 'Kafka protocol' (bad, confusion-inducing bureaucracy) to how attention and memory shape which ideas survive.

c2xdzOjakvw.title: A Protocol Fiction Protocol
c2xdzOjakvw.summary: Venkatesh Rao presents a theory of 'protocol fiction' as a genre distinct from both heroic fantasy (Ted Chiang's 'special people') and science fiction (Chiang's 'strange rules'), arguing it uniquely captures how humans transform alongside technological/institutional change rather than merely reacting to it or resisting it collectively (per Ursula Le Guin's 'carrier bag' model). He traces this through modernist literature, detective fiction, and Asimov/Dick/cyberpunk eras, then outlines three ways protocols appear in fiction (authorial process, central theme, background device), before Travis Van Epps and Sachin Benny discuss their own protocol-fiction writing experiments, including LLM ping-pong drafting techniques and story ideas drawn from DAO governance and care-package logistics in Venezuela.
key_concepts: protocol fiction as a genre distinct from heroic fantasy and classic sci-fi
Ted Chiang's 'strange rules vs. special people' distinction
three modes of protocols in fiction (authoring process, central theme, background device)
agency-in-system vs. agency-in-protagonist ('Bechdel test' for protocol fiction)

lQrETS1JnAw.title: AI as the Anti-product – Guest Talk with Peter Wang
lQrETS1JnAw.summary: Peter Wang (Anaconda co-founder, now Chief AI Officer, and founder of the Sky Seed fund) argues that modern software/AI development is best understood through a complexity-versus-complication lens: tool stacks like CUDA and PyTorch remain complicated (Boeing-747-style, decomposable) while the models and ecosystems they produce are genuinely complex and emergent, and 'vibe coding' represents a quasi-religious third mode of engaging code beyond craftsmanship and managerial industrialization. He traces how Anaconda/NumPy's open-source success came from humble, itch-scratching human ecologies (e.g. Travis Oliphant merging numeric and numarray into NumPy) rather than top-down design, and warns that protocols like AT Protocol/Blue Sky must avoid centralized 'technocratic' forced upgrades, instead preserving pluralistic values across nodes the way open source avoided forced EOL upgrades.
key_concepts: software 1.0 vs software 2.0 / vibe coding as prayerful practice
open-source ecosystems as organisms (Mississippi River metaphor)
protocols vs. apps (AT Protocol, Sky Seed fund)
forced upgrades and coherent pluralism in decentralized systems

-E1YnHpIfws.title: SoP 2025 Town Hall
-E1YnHpIfws.summary: Tim Beiko and Venkatesh Rao, co-directors of Summer of Protocols, recap the program's origins at the Ethereum Foundation and outline the 2025 theme of 'why' protocols matter (following prior years' 'what' and 'how'), structured around three tracks: education/curriculum grants, scene-making via the Protocolized magazine and protocol fiction contest, and technical foundations workshops in Bangkok. Rao frames the year's motto as 'accelerating order' against 'accelerating chaos,' invoking Gramsci's 'time of monsters' and Frankl's 'why' quote to argue protocols can address a broader meaning crisis, while Timber Stinson-Schroff moderates Q&A on curriculum grant requirements, protocol phenomenology (e.g., Nadia Asparouhova's 'CFKA protocol' concept), and distinctions between academic and corporate protocol teaching.
key_concepts: go big and go home / decentralized network model
CFKA vs Whitehead protocols (phenomenology of protocols)

KYTfwgZAvQ8.title: Memory Research Group
KYTfwgZAvQ8.summary: Keler (Kia) launches the Memory Research Group, a Summer of Protocols special interest group, outlining its focus on how memory concepts get conflated across neuroscience, computing, philosophy, and anthropology. She traces a lineage from Francis Yates's 'Art of Memory' and classical memory palaces through associative/taxonomic divides (Raymond Lull, Giordano Bruno) to contemporary bioelectric memory research (Michael Levin), Edwin Hutchins's distributed cognition, Buddhist models of memory as ethical construction, and Bernard Stiegler's technics-as-exteriorized-memory, arguing memory is fundamentally distributed across agents and environments rather than stored discretely.

ycSPyh8-G94.title: Plenary Talk - 2024 Protocol Symposium
ycSPyh8-G94.summary: Tim Beiko and Venkatesh Rao open the 2024 Protocol Symposium by recapping Summer of Protocols' two-year evolution, from testing whether 'protocols' form a coherent cross-domain field to this year's focus on applied stewardship, tensions (tradeoff plus conflict), and workshops like the Singapore and Edge Esmeralda pop-ups. Venkatesh then presents three orienting frameworks for the Symposium—the 'technological Tangled Bank,' the 'Erdos-Whitehead protocol age,' and the 'kit space of civilization'—arguing protocols are best understood as a literacy for seeing technology's relation to humans and environment rather than a technology class itself.
key_concepts: tensions (tradeoff + conflict) as a framework for protocol stewardship
Summer of Protocols program structure and research clusters

pK7U2IrPETQ.title: Guest Talk with Geoff Manaugh | Burglary, Architecture, and the Protocols of “Nakatomi Space”
pK7U2IrPETQ.summary: Geoff Manaugh, author of A Burglar's Guide to the City, argues that burglary is fundamentally an architectural and protocol-level phenomenon: criminals like the 'hole in the ground gang' and 'Roofman' exploit sufficiently granular knowledge of city infrastructure (storm drains, freeway on/off-ramps, fire codes, corporate franchise layouts) to identify repeatable spatial and temporal vulnerabilities. He develops the concept of 'Nakatomi Space' (named after Die Hard) as a parallel, hidden circulation system—air ducts, maintenance corridors, walls—that can be misused to move through buildings against their intended protocols, and discusses how rules meant to protect (fire code, corporate scheduling) simultaneously reveal how a system can be attacked.
key_concepts: seeing like a burglar (inversion of seeing like a state)

5gSh4biSvS8.title: Guest Talk with John Bissell | In Search of a Protocol for Matter (Dis)Assembly at Human Scale
5gSh4biSvS8.summary: John Bissell, CEO of Origin Materials, argues that the chemical industry lacks a robust protocol for developing new technologies and materials, unlike the highly predictable building-block system used for mass chemical production. He traces this to the computational intractability of quantum mechanics at human scale, illustrates it through the empirically-discovered Haber-Bosch ammonia synthesis, and surveys partial solutions like click chemistry, electrochemistry, synthetic biology, and Origin's own 'mechanical layer' approach of shifting material variability into structural engineering rather than new chemistry.
key_concepts: quantum mechanical incomputability at human scale
click chemistry and electrochemistry as predictive frameworks

dDEgt1-72YM.title: Research Salon with Kei Kreutler | Artificial Memory and Orienting Infinity
dDEgt1-72YM.summary: Kei Kreutler presents her Summer of Protocols research essay 'Artificial Memory and Orienting Infinity,' tracing a history of artificial memory from the method of loci and Renaissance memory theaters (Camillo, Giulio Bruno) through Turing machines and the invention of Random Access Memory. She introduces a framework distinguishing 'latent memory' from 'living memory' and 'taxonomic' from 'associative' arrangement, arguing for a sensibility she calls 'orientation' that enables navigating partial, associative cues rather than relying on the metaphor of memory-as-data.

SlXYIlpJRoY.title: Guest Talk with Chris Dixon | Read, Write, Own
SlXYIlpJRoY.summary: Chris Dixon discusses his book Read, Write, Own with Venkatesh Rao, arguing that blockchains represent a third type of network architecture—alongside 'protocol networks' (like HTTP/RSS) and 'corporate networks' (like Facebook)—that combines the societal benefits of open protocols with the competitive funding advantages of corporate platforms. He uses an extended city metaphor (public/private balance, logical vs. organizational decentralization) to explain why Web1 protocols stagnated due to lack of funding mechanisms, while blockchain networks like Ethereum and Farcaster enable 'composability' and persistent user ownership without centralized platform risk.
key_concepts: protocol networks vs corporate networks vs blockchain networks
composability and platform risk ('can't be evil')
digital ownership as the 'own' in Read, Write, Own
value creation vs value capture and token design
city metaphor for decentralized network governance

8LBZN1-T1fM.title: Guest Talk with Nils Gilman & Jonathan Blake | Planetary Subsidiarity
8LBZN1-T1fM.summary: Nils Gilman and Jonathan Blake of the Berggruen Institute present their book 'Children of a Modest Star,' arguing that planetary-scale problems like climate change and pandemics—phenomena that flow across borders independent of human intention—cannot be governed by the existing nation-state system or UN multilateralism. They propose a multiscalar governance architecture based on the principle of subsidiarity, where issues like climate mitigation are handled by new planetary institutions, adaptation is handled locally through translocal networks (e.g., Los Angeles collaborating with Cape Town rather than Miami), and the nation-state becomes a mediating 'meso-level' rather than the sovereign center, aiming for 'habitability' rather than mere 'sustainability.'

a9jQcvTC2Pw.title: Protocols for TV Comedy with Steve Hely
a9jQcvTC2Pw.summary: Steve Hely, a TV comedy writer and novelist, maps Hollywood's unwritten protocols onto the Summer of Protocols framework, walking through the pipeline from pitching (agents/managers, the five-part pitch structure, 'burglar ways' like South Park's demo tape) to the writer's room's 'yes and' norm, table reads as laughter-audits, and call-sheet production hierarchies. He argues comedy itself often arises from characters running mismatched protocols (Curb Your Enthusiasm, The Office, Big Bang Theory), and closes with skepticism that AI can yet replicate the emotional story-stakes that make scripted comedy work.
key_concepts: burglar ways of breaking into Hollywood

-uw9UiyvYBQ.title: Guest Talk with JoAnne Yates | The Trajectory of Global Standard Setting
-uw9UiyvYBQ.summary: JoAnne Yates, co-author of 'Engineering Rules,' traces three historical waves of private voluntary standard-setting from 1880 to today: the emergence of national bodies like BSI and IEC driven by figures like Charles le Maistre, the post-WWII rise of ISO as a global consensus-based leader, and the post-1980s fragmentation caused by competitors like IETF, corporate consortia, and W3C that challenge ISO's balanced-consensus model. She closes by questioning whether protocol-setting communities (e.g., Ethereum, coal mining safety) have developed the same cross-community coordination infrastructure that standards bodies built over a century.
key_concepts: national vs. international standards bodies (BSI, IEC, ISO)
corporate consortia vs. balanced stakeholder standardization

aQWZ50tIB98.title: Guest Talk with Renee DiResta | A Troll's Guide to the Internet
aQWZ50tIB98.summary: Renee DiResta traces how 'trolling' evolved from a good-natured in-group initiation ritual on early BBS and blog communities into a weaponized tactic used by state actors like Russia, ISIS, Turkey's AKP, and Pakistani and Tanzanian operatives who exploit platform design gaps and policy loopholes (e.g., fake DMCA takedowns, mass-reporting gamification, hacked accounts) before platforms develop corresponding moderation protocols. She argues social platforms are designed for 'best case' use, creating a persistent gap between technological design affordances and reactive content-moderation policy, and discusses the historical collapse of the distinction between 'propaganda machine' (one-to-many broadcast) and 'rumor mill' (peer-to-peer salience-driven spread) in the social media era. She closes by weighing whether decentralized, federated protocols (Mastodon, Bluesky's AT Protocol) can offset this dynamic given they lack the large-scale moderation infrastructure of major platforms.</summary_truncated>
key_concepts: trolling evolution from in-group ritual to weaponized tactic
design vs. policy protocols in platform moderation
propaganda machine vs. rumor mill collapse

AgVfb5ytx9Y.title: Guest Talk with Bryan Johnson | The Blueprint Protocol
AgVfb5ytx9Y.summary: In an interview format with Venkatesh Rao, Bryan Johnson describes his Blueprint Protocol—a self-experimentation regime using extensive biomarker measurement, strict diet (2000 calories, vegan, 11am last meal), supplement 'survival of the fittest' testing, and sleep optimization—to reverse his biological aging. Johnson also discusses his 'evening Brian vs. morning Brian' internal-personas framework for behavioral control, his brain-interface company Kernel's spectroscopy-based brain-age measurement, and his evolving personal philosophy that 'don't die' is the only meaningful species-level objective given emerging AI superintelligence.
key_concepts: don't-die philosophy / AI alignment with human longevity

u_mU4Io2s1w.title: Guest Talk with Alex Komoroske | Gardening Platforms
u_mU4Io2s1w.summary: Alex Komoroske, drawing on his experience leading Chrome's web platform team, argues that platforms should be 'gardened' rather than engineered: built incrementally and horizontally from adjacent possible use cases rather than vertically toward a single predetermined goal, with continuous 'rationalization' to pay down the debt that inevitably accumulates as platform and ecosystem co-evolve. He frames platforms and their ecosystems as living, symbiotic systems bound by a 'gravitational pull' that breaks if changes move too fast, and discusses how platforms die through ossification, rising coordination costs, or failed 'second system' rewrites. In Q&A he extends the framework to crypto protocols, corporate digital transformation, and security-by-design, debating with Toby Shorin and others how legal/organizational fragmentation changes platform dynamics in permissionless networks like Ethereum, Cosmos, and Solana.
key_concepts: coordination headwinds / metabolic rate of debt
gravitational pull and co-evolution of platform and ecosystem
security posture and trust in platform design

Ju9DewoTyx4.title: Protocol Town Hall with Gordon Brander | Noosphere: A Protocol for Thought
Ju9DewoTyx4.summary: Gordon Brander presents Noosphere, a decentralized protocol built on IPFS for a 'worldwide decentralized shared mind,' contrasting the original utopian vision of the web (Tim Berners-Lee, Ted Nelson, Engelbart) with the centralized, siloed Web 2.0 shaped by network effects, zero marginal cost, returns to scale, and same-origin security. He argues self-certifying protocols (rooted in user-held cryptographic keys rather than server authority) can restore composability and 'credible exit,' describing concepts like memos, spheres, UCANs, and a solution to Zuko's Triangle via hyperlocal naming, with Subconscious as the first client application. In Q&A, he debates with Kartik, Dorian Taylor, and Venkatesh Rao about whether zero marginal cost truly holds, inevitable centralization (mining pools, email oligopolies), and how UCAN-based key delegation and social recovery can mitigate the trade-off between decentralization and usability.
key_concepts: network effects, zero marginal cost, and same-origin security policy

9Cs9Yf6WpUk.title: Protocol Town Hall with David Lang | Standards Make the World
9Cs9Yf6WpUk.summary: David Lang presents his Summer of Protocols research on standards-making, drawing on his experience co-founding OpenROV and later developing the Bristlemouth underwater connector standard at Sofar Ocean. He argues standards fall into distinct types (safety, interoperability, performance, contractual) and traces three historical waves of standards-making per Yates and Murphy's 'Engineering Rules,' proposing that a 'disruptive model' of standards creation—where outsiders build working solutions first and backfill institutional approval later, as seen with CubeSats, MIDI, and BioBricks—is replacing the traditional top-down consortial model.
key_concepts: types of standards (safety, interoperability, performance, contractual)

cgqJNo5taLI.title: Research Salon with Rafael Fernández | The Swarm and the Formation
cgqJNo5taLI.summary: Rafael Fernández presents his summer protocols research 'The Swarm and the Formation,' arguing that digital swarms—networks of people, content, and bots coordinated through algorithms rather than explicit protocols—emerge precisely in the absence of protocol, using the 2017 Puerto Rico hurricane Mutual Aid response and the Silicon Valley Bank collapse as case studies. He proposes a taxonomy distinguishing swarms from crowds, guerrillas, mimetic tribes, digital farms, online communities, and encoded virtual organizations (e.g., MakerDAO), mapped along a spectrum from unprotocolized 'terrain-driven' coordination to fully encoded social protocols, and introduces concepts like 'emergent promise,' swarm life cycles modeled on hurricanes, and 'attunement technologies' (like Community Notes) as an alternative to assimilationist alignment.
key_concepts: swarm vs. crowd vs. guerrilla vs. mimetic tribe taxonomy
terrain as protocol / absence of protocol

Q56q9Eq9bnA.title: Researcher Salon with Kara Kittel & Toby Shorin | Unprotocolized Knowleldge
Q56q9Eq9bnA.summary: Kara Kittel and Toby Shorin present their Summer of Protocols research 'Unprotocolized Knowledge,' tracing how their original focus on internet authorship norms evolved into a study of 'credit cultures' and ultimately a framework for how knowledge legitimacy is produced outside formal academic protocols. They map a spectrum from protocol-delimited academic knowledge to unmediated social epistemology, using case studies like the seed oil wars, Alzheimer's amyloid hypothesis stagnation, and TikTok neurodivergence research to argue for new bridging protocols between citizen science, populist paradigms, and institutional peer review.

84aDDKv4nPM.title: Guest Talk with Jay Graber | Q&A Hosted by Venkatesh Rao
84aDDKv4nPM.summary: Jay Graber (CEO) and Daniel Holmgren (Protocol Lead) of Bluesky discuss building the AT Protocol as a 'hybrid' alternative to both maximalist peer-to-peer decentralization and traditional centralized platforms, emphasizing that decentralization is 'a function of administrative control, not network topology' (quoting advisor Martin Kleppmann). They explain concepts like self-certifying repositories (DIDs, PDS), stackable/composable moderation as 'building blocks' rather than monolithic trust-and-safety, and contrast their 'schematic web' schema approach (Lexicon) with RDF/semantic web ontologies, arguing protocol entrepreneurship requires balancing fast app iteration with slow, methodical protocol design.
key_concepts: decentralization as administrative control vs. topology
Lexicon schema language vs. RDF/semantic web

OEJXl2jibSI.title: Salon I: End-to-End Encryption in ActivityPub - 2024 Protocol Symposium
OEJXl2jibSI.summary: Evan Prodromou and Tom Coates present their Summer of Protocols research on integrating end-to-end encryption into ActivityPub, arguing that the fediverse's low-trust server operators and high-risk user base (LGBTQ users, activists, infosec community) make E2E encryption necessary despite the protocol's original email-like trust assumptions. They explain why they chose Messaging Layer Security (MLS) over alternatives like PGP, Signal's protocol, or OTR—citing MLS's royalty-free IETF standard status and scalability—and propose a new ActivityPub extension adding a key store and groups mechanism, while Coates details UI challenges around key management, archive restoration, and segregating encrypted from unencrypted messages.

YUNhWqMbNAk.title: Salon II: ARC Regenerative Communities - 2024 Protocol Symposium
YUNhWqMbNAk.summary: Kaliya Young and 'day' present research into the Internet Engineering Task Force (IETF) as a case study in regenerative governance, tracing its origins from the 1969 ARPANET through the 1992 governance crisis that shifted power from Vint Cerf's 'kitchen cabinet' IAB to open working groups organized around 'rough consensus and running code.' They map IETF practices—nomcom's randomized leadership selection, open RFC documentation, dispatch meetings, and ritualized in-person gatherings—onto three pattern languages (Group Works, Wise Democracy, and Social Permaculture) to argue that openness, transparency, and voluntariness are structural necessities, not limitations, for sustaining a healthy digital commons.

xGt2HCBS-fE.title: Salon III: Shoreline Adaptations to Urban Flooding - 2024 Protocol Symposium
xGt2HCBS-fE.summary: Celeste LeCompte and Danielle Butler present their Protocol Symposium research project on shoreline adaptation to urban flooding, arguing that current flood-management protocols are rigid because they encode an implicit framing of risk measured in capital terms, which forecloses opportunity-based alternatives. Drawing on Nadia Asparouhova's 'dangerous protocols' and Drew Austin's 'protocols don't build pyramids,' they catalog informal interventions (sewer-tunnel concerts, canoe clubs, Clean Water Act contact-standard pressure) as ways to disrupt entrenched disconnection between cities and water, and propose a database/questionnaire tool to analyze which design features make such interventions effective at shifting culture toward managed retreat and integrated adaptation.
key_concepts: risk vs. opportunity framing in flood protocols
managed retreat and seeding land back to water
Clean Water Act primary/secondary contact standards as galvanizing protocol leverage

snnk_8q1w_4.title: Salon IV: Plurality in Practice - 2024 Protocol Symposium
snnk_8q1w_4.summary: Rich McDowell and Ben (surname not given) present findings from their Protocol Institute orienteering grant studying plural voting mechanisms, including a real-world CCM (connection-oriented cluster match) experiment run at a crypto mechanism-design conference to allocate research grants. They identify a mathematical flaw in standard CCM where adding multiple identity dimensions breaks the property that the model should converge to quadratic voting when no groupings exist, propose a deduplication fix, and detail practical failures of Pol.is for generating grouping dimensions, including opaque dimension-reduction and missing-value interpolation causing confusion among participants.
key_concepts: pairwise quadratic voting / liquid democracy interactions

xIJP3Dtj7Sc.title: Salon V: Autonomous Realities - 2024 Protocol Symposium
xIJP3Dtj7Sc.summary: Amber Hu presents research on 'autonomous realities,' the fragmentation of shared experience as personalized mixed-reality (AR/VR) devices proliferate, and proposes a 'decentralized digital chemistry' framework using self-sovereign identity (DIDs) and object capabilities to let people merge disparate mixed-reality worlds when they physically encounter each other. The talk also introduces multi-party computation and private set intersection as a protocol for detecting mutual interest in merging realities before an encounter, illustrated by a planned art piece called 'Quantum Masquerade' for Defcon. Attendees including Dorian and others raise engineering concerns about decentralized access control and cultural parallels to etiquette-based reality negotiation.
key_concepts: multi-party computation and private set intersection for intent-matching
digital chemistry metaphor for merging autonomous realities

ZcnI_ErQoV8.title: Salon VI: Fire Protocols & Attention as Autopoietic Space - 2024 Protocol Symposium
ZcnI_ErQoV8.summary: Jiordi Rosales and Nathalia Scherer present their Summer of Protocols research on wildfire and prescribed-burn coordination in Sonoma County, California, framing fire management through the lens of autopoiesis—protocols as active matter that let communities regenerate fire knowledge rather than suppress it. They detail a concrete proposal adopted by the Good Fire Alliance to create regional burn coordinators housed under legitimate funded organizations (like Fire Forward), address land-owner bottlenecks, and reposition 'local knowledge keepers' over absentee landowners as fire experts, alongside a pocket logbook artifact for tracking weather and fire-return intervals.
key_concepts: legibility and institutional legitimacy for grassroots fire organizations

28DpSJYQKXk.title: Researcher Salon with Sarah Friend | Good Death
28DpSJYQKXk.summary: Sarah Friend presents her Summer of Protocols research 'Good Death,' arguing that protocols and digital worlds (MMOs, blockchains, NFT projects) don't have a binary alive/dead state but undergo a liminal 'dying' process followed by a social decision of death, analogous to the historical evolution of medical death diagnosis (heart death vs. brain death) and anthropological rites of passage. She introduces Venkatesh Rao's concept of 'world' as what grows atop a protocol, examines memorials embedded in blockchains (e.g., Hal Finney-style tributes), dead-blockchain lists, and Ethereum's difficulty bomb as a case of engineered protocol mortality, closing with questions about what archives or memorials are appropriate for dead digital worlds.
key_concepts: world (per Venkatesh Rao's worlding framework) as what grows on a protocol
death as process vs. death as decision (liminal/liminal state)
brain death and legal/social death analogies applied to protocols
dead blockchain lists and 'order of protological death'
Ethereum difficulty bomb as momento mori / protocol mortality mechanism

YcBl43ziHKE.title: Protocol Town Hall with Chenoe Hart | Addressable Space
YcBl43ziHKE.summary: Chenoe Hart presents her Summer of Protocols research project 'Addressable Space,' tracing how built environments are remapped through informational systems — from 18th-century European house-numbering schemes that decoupled addresses from physical geography, to skipped floor numbers and hidden 'mechanical voids' in skyscrapers, to elevators as random-access devices. She argues these spatial protocols reshape human experience much like digital file systems, and calls for 'protocol empathy' — the practice of imagining how built space appears from a protocol's or computer system's point of view.

GtHp7DVt3jQ.title: Protocol Town Hall Salon with Angela Walch | The Protocol System Experience
GtHp7DVt3jQ.summary: Angela Walch, a former law professor and Summer of Protocols researcher, presents her framework 'The Protocol System Experience,' which maps an individual's (personified as 'Pip') journey through any protocol system—from blockchains to families to religions—using concepts like well-being (thriving vs. dysphoria), fit, and autonomy. She argues that autonomy requires both awareness (seeing the 'water' you swim in) and insight (deep knowledge of power dynamics), and introduces terms like 'protocol determinism,' 'protocol overhang,' and 'protocol scars' to describe how membership in one system compels or haunts behavior in others.
key_concepts: fit between self and protocol role

Z0-mcmZcTuU.title: SoP Researcher Salon with Timber Schroff | Safe New World
Z0-mcmZcTuU.summary: Timber Schroff presents his Summer of Protocols research essay 'Safe New World,' analyzing a 97% decline in coal mining fatalities from 1900-2000 to build a general theory of protocol evolution driven by mutation (errors in replication, perception, and storage) and selection pressures like influence, feedback speed, and bandwidth. He argues safety protocols have largely 'solved' acute workplace harm, while health protocols addressing chronic disease (heart disease, black lung, COPD) remain the unsolved frontier, and proposes 'tinkering' with existing protocols as the optimal path for protocol innovation rather than top-down design.
key_concepts: tinkering vs. design vs. mutation in protocol creation

0gC5Dd1mtDA.title: Researcher Salon with Dorian Taylor| Retrofitting the Web
0gC5Dd1mtDA.summary: Dorian Taylor presents 'Intertwiler,' his Summer of Protocols project to build a hypermedia engine that fixes the web's broken transclusion, unstable URLs, and one-directional linking by treating links and resources as typed, first-class objects governed by open protocols rather than proprietary software. Drawing on decades of personal history—from 1990s BBS art scenes and dot-com personal websites to Ted Nelson's hypertext theory, Horst Rittel's issue-based information systems, and Christopher Alexander's design theory—Taylor argues that most information systems fail because they try to contain all information internally rather than defining interoperable conventions, and demonstrates a live (buggy) prototype using RDF, RDFa, and XSLT to achieve seamless, protocol-based content transclusion.

dsO8DwV0eaQ.title: Protocol Town Hall with Yancey Strickler | When the Means Justify the Ends
dsO8DwV0eaQ.summary: Yancey Strickler, co-founder of Kickstarter, recounts Metalabel's two-year journey building crypto-based infrastructure for creative 'culture labels' inspired by punk record labels and the Royal Society, and how repeated crises (the Gitcoin/Vitalik NFT frenzy, Pepe coin gas spikes, and a wallet drain) led the team to go on a 'crypto diet' and ultimately launch Metalabel with zero blockchains underneath, borrowing crypto's values (decentralized identifiers, open data, shared financial outcomes) while prioritizing end-user experience over ideological means. He argues crypto culture often lets 'the means justify the ends,' making it a poor 'major' but potentially a good 'minor' within a broader post-platform, protocol-literate design space, a point Venkatesh Rao extends with his 'brains, trains, and vibes-mobiles' metaphor.
key_concepts: means vs. ends in protocol design
crypto diet / climbing out of the rabbit hole

ne7Dxj4KvQ4.title: Protocol Town Hall with Venkatesh Rao | Formulating a Protocol Pill
ne7Dxj4KvQ4.summary: Venkatesh Rao, program lead for Summer of Protocols, synthesizes the 2023 research cohort's output and proposes 'formulating a protocol pill' — a deliberate, effectuation-driven strategy (starting from available assets rather than goals) to spread 'protocol literacy' as a cognitive shift from 'I am my protocols' to 'I have protocols,' using Robert Kegan's developmental-stages framework. He outlines the components of a 'kit' (attitude elixir, modes of agency, aesthetic sensibility, collective memory orientation, escapist comfort, local conditions) needed to grow a 'protocol scene' akin to the maker movement, referencing Josh Stark's concept of 'hardness,' Nadia Asparouhova's work on protocols as dual-use technologies, and plans to pivot 2024 research toward applications and oblique attacks on problems like AI safety and climate change.
key_concepts: I am vs I have (Kegan developmental levels)

ihn5FmlXDmo.title: Guest Talk with Jesse Walden | Contract Theory and Protocol Design
ihn5FmlXDmo.summary: Jesse Walden (Variant VC, co-founder of Media Chain) presents a framework derived from Oliver Hart's contract theory, distinguishing 'complete' protocols (simple, deterministic, trust-minimized, automated — e.g. Bitcoin, Uniswap v1) from 'incomplete' protocols that require ongoing human governance and interpretation (e.g. Aave, Nouns DAO, MolochDAO's rage-quit mechanism). He argues many crypto projects fall into an 'uncanny valley' by claiming completeness/decentralization they don't actually have, and points to Uniswap v4's hooks as a hybrid model that automates a complete core while delegating customization to the market. Discussion with Tim, Angela Walch, and others explores whether true completeness is ever attainable, the role of tokens as 'economic alignment' products, and regulatory incentives (SEC's 'sufficient decentralization') that pressure projects to overclaim completeness.

6eaQNbwYUJE.title: Guest Talk with Jason Morton | Unpacking Money as a Protocol
6eaQNbwYUJE.summary: Jason Morton, a researcher working on zero-knowledge proofs (via his project Ezekiel/EZKL), argues that money-as-ledger is a leaky, obsolete abstraction and proposes three reframings: bank balances as a one-dimensional zero-knowledge proof compressing all past favors; money as 'fuzzy ownership' modeled via Dirichlet/beta distributions that let communities tune ambiguity versus precision in claims on shared resources; and balances as an impossible projection of 3+1 dimensional Minkowski spacetime onto a single global zero-dimensional ledger, which breaks down given compute speeds now rivaling light-speed limits. He floats speculative alternatives—an 'AI St. Peter' judging favors without money, a Dirichlet-distribution-based ownership pool, and an urn-based 'Archer net' protocol using randomized balls to achieve statistical indistinguishability across unsynced nodes—as thought experiments rather than finished proposals.
key_concepts: Minkowski spacetime projection and double-spend as causal risk

fJNEJdRKRJ4.title: Guest Talk with Scott Moore | This Session is Not Legitimate: An Exploration of Social Rule-Making
fJNEJdRKRJ4.summary: Scott Moore (GitCoin co-founder) explores Vitalik Buterin's framework on legitimacy, walking through six sources of legitimacy—brute force/coercion, continuity, process, performance, participation, and fairness—and ranking them from weakest to strongest. He applies these lenses to case studies like PGP's path to legitimacy and EIP-1559's contentious adoption, and closes by questioning whether legitimacy itself can be formalized as a protocol, invoking Gödel's incompleteness and Asimov's robotics laws as cautionary analogies.
key_concepts: brute force vs. process vs. participation legitimacy
EIP-1559 and PGP as case studies

Z9O5_lve10o.title: Guest Talk with Trent Van Epps | Capital and Enclosure in Software Commons: Linux & Ethereum
Z9O5_lve10o.summary: Trent Van Epps, researcher at the Ethereum Foundation and steward of Protocol Guild, presents a framework distinguishing capital and commons modes of production, then applies it to case studies of Linux (and Red Hat's gradual enclosure of CentOS) and Ethereum. He argues Ethereum is unique among software commons because it contains embedded capital circuits (proof-of-stake ETH, MEV, liquid staking) and produces a single globally-bound state object, raising the question of whether this containment stabilizes or dooms the commons to capture, and proposes Protocol Guild's unaffiliated funding model as a partial countermeasure.
key_concepts: commons vs. capital modes of production
embedded capital circuits in Ethereum L1

JqCnuFMummk.title: Guest Talk with Simone Cicero | Perspectives on the Platforms vs Protocols Debate: A Reality Check
JqCnuFMummk.summary: Simone Cicero presents a systematic comparison of platform and protocol business models, arguing that platforms derive value from a triad of product, marketplace, and extensibility features while protocols can theoretically deliver equivalent or better value propositions but suffer from weaker defensibility and immature go-to-market organizational doctrine. He proposes that protocols may extract revenue legitimately only when they maintain stateful representations and run infrastructural functions, and discusses cases like ONDC in India where policy enforcement, not organic competition, solves the bootstrapping problem.
key_concepts: innovation cycles and commoditization of complements
stateful vs networkless protocols and fee extraction
vertical unbundling and the unbundling fallacy

1Y9ZuyiwAqc.title: Guest Talk with Ian Cheng | Neuro Gym
1Y9ZuyiwAqc.summary: Ian Cheng traces his evolution as an artist from early raw motion-capture work ('This Papaya Tastes Perfect') through self-playing simulations ('Entropy Wrangler', 'Emissaries') to the AI-driven creature Bob, built using Richard Evans' neurosymbolic inductive logic programming to model belief-formation and motivated perception. He discusses colliding scripted narrative with open-ended simulation, drawing on Dramatica story theory, Jeff Hawkins' thousand-brains model of mind, and Will Wright's systems-based design philosophy to explain his approach to AI-generated worlds and storytelling in works like 'Life After Bob'.
key_concepts: neurosymbolic inductive logic programming (Richard Evans' model)
thousand brains / cortical column theory of mind (Jeff Hawkins)
simulation vs. scripted story as colliding sculptural forces

kWPpprIjpwA.title: Guest Talk with Mike Masnick | The Role of Protocols in Decentralization
kWPpprIjpwA.summary: Mike Masnick traces the evolution of his thinking since his 2019 'Protocols, Not Platforms' paper, engaging criticisms from Moxie Marlinspike (that protocols are too slow and prone to corporate capture) and reframing decentralization not as an absolute good but as a question of which system components should be centralized versus pushed to the edges. Using the U.S. interstate highway system as an analogy, he argues the protocol itself should function as a stable, centralized foundation while competition and innovation happen in decentralized nodes built on top of it, and discusses how Twitter's Musk acquisition and Bluesky's emergence illustrate these dynamics in practice.
key_concepts: decentralization as incentive structure rather than end goal

d6BDMO0JqXI.title: Guest Talk with Chen Qiufan | Science Fiction as Protocol
d6BDMO0JqXI.summary: Author Chen Qiufan (Stanley Chan) argues that science fiction functions as a protocol for reconciling heterogeneous systems of thought, drawing on his own experiments training an AI writing collaborator ('Chen Qiufan 2.0') to explore distributed and non-centralized models of cognition found in novels like Peter Watts' Blindsight, Vernor Vinge's A Fire Upon the Deep, and Ursula K. Le Guin's work. He proposes that symbiosis and endosymbiosis—biological precedents for merging distinct systems—offer a template for how carbon-based and silicon-based intelligence might coexist, framing science fiction as a tool to counterbalance cognitive asymmetry and motivate participation in shaping the future.

MnLUqtceQzA.title: Guest Talk with Janine Leger | Zuzalu: A First of Its Kind IRL Pop-up Community
MnLUqtceQzA.summary: Janine Leger, organizer of Zuzalu, presents the two-month pop-up community experiment in Montenegro (200 residents, 600+ visitors, funded largely by Vitalik Buterin) as a case study in deliberate community design, highlighting principles like proximity, kindness/curiosity as trust-building culture, decentralized social tech (zoopass, zuzalu.city scheduling), rituals, and local integration with Montenegrin officials. She draws explicit parallels to the Summer of Protocols cohort, urging the researchers to adopt similar practices—small core teams relying on broader groups, visitor rotation to avoid insularity, public 'dogfooding' of in-progress work, and rituals—to build a sustainable, collaborative research community.
key_concepts: core team vs. residents vs. visitors ratio

Ve5W7C3AxvY.title: Guest Talk with Dara O'Rourke | How to Blow Up a Carbon Data Pipeline
Ve5W7C3AxvY.summary: Dara O'Rourke, professor of sustainability sciences at Berkeley, argues that mainstream carbon protocols like the Greenhouse Gas Protocol, CDP, and Science Based Targets initiative have become 'up and out' external reporting systems that are easily gamed and fail to drive actual decarbonization, citing CDP's own finding that only 0.4% of reporting firms have credible decarbonization plans. Drawing on his six years building Amazon's internal carbon system of record (with Venkatesh Rao), he proposes shifting to 'down and in' actionable input metrics—like grams of CO2 per unit shipped—embedded directly into company optimization algorithms for procurement, routing, and R&D, rather than annual aggregate disclosures.
key_concepts: carbon system of record / internal carbon intelligence
science-based targets and CDP reporting gaming
Montreal Protocol vs Kyoto Protocol effectiveness
input metrics vs output metrics for corporate decarbonization

JsRuk6wu-0Y.title: Guest Talk with Kazys Varnelis | The City as Communications System
JsRuk6wu-0Y.summary: Kazys Varnelis traces the architectural and infrastructural history of communication networks, arguing that cities are themselves communication systems whose physical form has been shaped by protocols ranging from post offices and telegraph hubs to Cold War-era microwave relay systems like AT&T's long lines. He contrasts Paul Baran's theoretical 'distributed' network model with the 'decentralized' hub-and-spoke reality of actual infrastructure (exemplified by buildings like 33 Thomas Street and One Wilshire), concluding that protocols are not just abstract rule-sets but physically and legally embedded in urban space, and that cities and protocols co-shape each other in a cybernetic feedback loop.
key_concepts: distributed vs. decentralized vs. centralized networks (Paul Baran)
the data center's historical lineage from post offices and telegraph buildings
long lines microwave network and Cold War infrastructure protocols
physical/legal protocols embedded in urban infrastructure (building codes, right-of-way, telecom regulation)

-8JJARAI6ak.title: Guest Talk with Matt Webb | Fiction, Desire, and Belief
-8JJARAI6ak.summary: Matt Webb builds on his earlier essay 'Who Could Write Protocol Fiction' by arguing that protocol designers must deliberately engineer belief and desire, not just reference implementations, drawing on Gabriel Tarde's sociology (imitation and imposition as the only social forces), Dave Winer's 'Rules for Standards Makers,' and design fiction's use of charismatic material artifacts as boundary objects. He illustrates this with Stripe's 'seven lines of code' onboarding and 1950s science fiction's 'consensus cosmogony' of space exploration, then leads a workshop where participants invent protocols (anti-spam payment-gated messaging, death/grief archiving rituals, hazard-alert networks, and the Bristlemouth marine hardware standard) and brainstorm artifacts to generate belief and desire for each.

UAtt1F7fMLE.title: Guest Talk with Kyle Mathews | Designing for Soft Protocols: A Discord Bot Workshop
UAtt1F7fMLE.summary: Kyle Mathews, introduced by Venkatesh Rao (referred to as 'vanet'), led a hands-on workshop distinguishing 'hard protocols' (rigid, software-enforced, testable like Greenhouse's hiring flow) from 'soft protocols' (governing, influence-based, running partly in human 'wetware' like Twitter's emergent norms). Participants broke into small groups to design a Discord bot for bookmarking/sharing links within the Summer of Protocols community, producing user stories around prioritization, auto-tagging, digests, and feeds, followed by reflections (notably from David Lang and Cara) questioning whether such categorization tools would actually be adopted or whether the exercise merely reinforced existing Discord-centric work patterns.
key_concepts: Discord bot for link bookmarking and categorization
worse-is-better / early adopter approach to protocol design

MUfqF_3fghE.title: Guest Talk with Cory Levinson | Who Writes the Rules of Climate Protocols?
MUfqF_3fghE.summary: Cory Levinson traces the history of carbon markets from the Kyoto Protocol through the Paris Agreement's still-unoperationalized Article 6.4, contrasting the fragmented voluntary carbon market (Verra, Gold Standard, ACR) with compliance regimes, and recounts how Toucan's CO2 (CLA) tokenization protocol exploited Verra's retirement mechanism until Verra froze bridging in 2022. He then frames climate protocols into three layers—financial, scientific (MRV/methodologies), and semantic (ontologies/RDF)—arguing that semantic protocols using relational data models like RDF and the semantic web could let disparate scientific methodologies build on each other rather than scaling in isolation.
key_concepts: Article 6.4 compliance vs. voluntary carbon markets
semantic protocols and RDF/ontologies for ecological data
permanence, additionality, and leakage risk in offsets

PW3nOUwIRpY.title: Guest Talk with Varun Srinivasan | Technology & Architecture
PW3nOUwIRpY.summary: Varun Srinivasan, CTO and co-founder of Farcaster, discusses the architecture of Farcaster and its commercial client Warpcast, tracing his path from Coinbase to building a decentralized social protocol. He details the concept of 'sufficient decentralization' (the test that two users must always be able to communicate even if the rest of the network tries to stop them), explains why Farcaster pivoted from a Federated model to a hybrid blockchain-identity approach, and describes how the 'Frames' feature emerged by extending the Open Graph protocol to embed interactive mini-apps directly in the social feed.
key_concepts: Federated vs client P2P vs blockchain decentralization models

C0yDi7VnLrU.title: Guest Talk with Sarah Perry | Protocols of Reproducible Science
C0yDi7VnLrU.summary: Sarah Perry argues that most social-science abstract nouns—aggression, humility, the subconscious—are 'weasel words' whose laboratory operationalizations (the Bobo doll, Taylor aggression paradigm, self-report surveys) are so varied and arbitrary that they fail to measure anything generalizable, a pattern she calls 'protocol as alibi' where following procedure substitutes for real knowledge. She contrasts this with 'protocol as checksum,' where minor, publicly checkable procedural details (IRB approval, properly sourced gel images, unmanipulated data files) serve as tells for whether hidden parts of a study were actually done honestly, illustrated through cases like Hwang Woo-suk's cloning fraud and Dan Ariely's disputed honesty and placebo studies. Venkatesh Rao introduces the talk by linking Perry's earlier ribbonfarm writing on architecture and ritual to her current focus on reproducibility and the generalizability crisis.

i--HcD5Zx-A.title: Guest Talk with Evan Miyazono | Putting Protocols into Practice
i--HcD5Zx-A.summary: Evan Miyazono, head of research at Protocol Labs, walks through his mechanism-design approach to protocols—mapping rules to strategies to outcomes—using Filecoin's proof-of-replication and the late addition of Filecoin Plus (a trust layer to prevent 'useless bit' storage attacks) as a case study. He then surveys Protocol Labs' public-goods funding experiments (hypercerts, retroactive funding, the S-process for preference aggregation, Funding the Commons conferences) and closes with speculative thoughts on open agency architecture for AI alignment as a future protocol challenge.
key_concepts: hypercerts and retroactive public goods funding

Z4Sy9OZjuOQ.title: Guest Talk with Daniel Bashir | A Survey of AI for the Protocol-Minded
Z4Sy9OZjuOQ.summary: Daniel Bashir, ML engineer at AWS and host of The Gradient podcast, surveys how protocol thinking applies across AI—from funding and scaling laws (like DeepMind's Chinchilla compute-optimal training protocol) to benchmarks (perplexity vs. François Chollet's ARC benchmark for measuring sample-efficient generalization) to regulation (the EU AI Act's risk-tiered categorization). He argues that nearly every layer of AI development—research, engineering, deployment, and governance—can be reframed as a set of competing or evolving protocols, using examples like Sarah Hooker's 'hardware lottery' and Tolga Bolukbasi-style debates over fair/responsible AI operationalization.
key_concepts: scaling laws and the bitter lesson
benchmarks as protocols (perplexity, ARC, vibe-based evaluation)
Chollet's formal definition of intelligence and generalization hierarchy
